report.headline: Usage rate projected to fall to 14.4% in the NBA, well below the league's 20.1% average, while the shooting‑efficiency projection carries no signal.

projection.text: The model projects a usage rate of 14.4% in the NBA, down from 17.8% in the G League, against a league average of 20.1% and standard deviation of 5.2% — roughly 1.1 standard deviations below the typical NBA regular. The 80% interval (9.2%–19.7%) spans about two full standard deviations of the receiving league, meaning the model can say this usage will likely be below average but cannot pin down where within that range.

risks.text: Almost no three-point volume in the source season (0.7% of attempts), which raises doubt about floor-spacing value in an NBA role.
A relatively high turnover rate of 16.9% in the source season.

Usage is projected to shrink from 17.8% to 14.4%, roughly a full standard deviation below the NBA average of 20.1%, consistent with the general pattern of shrinking roles on the move up, though the 80% interval (9.2%–19.7%) is wide enough to include roughly average usage as well.
The true-shooting projection is built on a model that underperforms a simple league-average baseline for this transition, so no efficiency conclusion can be drawn from it.

strengths.text: Strong rebounding production in the source season, at 13.182 rebounds per 75 possessions.
Secondary playmaking activity, with 3.014 assists per 75 possessions and a 12.4% assist rate.
The projection is anchored in a reasonably substantial season of production — 44 games and 1,469 minutes — rather than a small sample.

uncertainty.text: The true-shooting projection of 51.8% should not be treated as informative: its out-of-fold error (4.7%) is no better than simply guessing the league-mean true-shooting percentage (also 4.7%), so the model loses to a trivial baseline on this metric for this transition type.
